facts.statement: The genus Palaeotringa was described by O. C. Marsh in 1870.
Remains of Palaeotringa were found in the Hornerstown Formation of New Jersey, straddling the Cretaceous-Paleocene boundary approximately 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Its remains were found in the controversial Hornerstown Formation of New Jersey (United States) which straddles the Cretaceous-Paleocene boundary some 66 million years ago.

facts.statement: Palaeotringa were initially thought to be primitive Gruiformes but were later classified in the form taxon Graculavidae, known as "transitional shorebirds".
facts.quote: They were for some time believed to be primitive, small Gruiformes and later on placed in the form taxon "Graculavidae", the "transitional shorebirds".

facts.statement: It is debated whether Palaeotringa belongs to Charadriiformes or is a basal member of Neoaves near the common ancestor of cranes, rails, storks, and herons.
facts.quote: Instead of being Charadriiformes, they might be some distinct but rather basal member of the Neoaves, close to the common ancestor of some or all of such birds as cranes, rails, storks and/or herons perhaps.

facts.statement: The parent group of Palaeotringa is the family Graculavidae.
The type species of the genus Palaeotringa is Palaeotringa littoralis.
Palaeotringa lived from the Maastrichtian to the Danian stages, between 72.2 and 61.66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Danian (72.2 to 61.66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Two species are currently assigned to the genus Palaeotringa: P. littoralis and P. vagans.
facts.quote: Two species are assigned to this genus nowadays, Palaeotringa littoralis and P. vagans.

facts.statement: The remains of Palaeotringa are too fragmentary for precise cladistic analysis, though they are confirmed as Neornithes.
facts.quote: Their remains are too fragmentary for cladistic analysis to say anything more precise than that they are Neornithes like all birds alive today.
